newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD signals compromise in German tax bill row.
newsitem.headline: SPD signals compromise in German tax bill row.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrat (SPD) opposition on Thursday signalled readiness to compromise with the government in a tax row where agreement could influence chances for pushing through sweeping tax reforms later.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition government has been deadlocked with the SPD -- which can block tax measures with its majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament -- over the passage of the 1997 tax bill.
But SPD tax negotiator, Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau, told reporters he may now drop his demand for the wealth tax to be scrapped and allow the bill instead to pass.
Offering a face-saving compromise, Voscherau said the wealth tax -- ruled illegal by the constitutional court -- would disappear automatically next year and was not a part of the tax bill.
Government and opposition parties are seeking a compromise in parliament's mediation process -- which handles deadlocked measures. It met on Thursday and should prepare a final report by December 5.
Voscherau, who said he still favoured taxing private fortunes, warned he would only make his position final next week after talking to his SPD colleagues.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax bill makes changes to state revenue. His budget, due for a final parliamentary vote on Friday, governs federal spending.

The combined package is intended to make Germany qualify for European monetary union with a deficit at 2.5 percent of gross domestic product next year -- below the Maastricht treaty's three percent limit.

Earlier this week, Kohl's Christian Democratic Party (CDU) threatened to let the tax bill fail in the face of the SPD blocking strategy -- which could have resulted in the loss of billions of marks of revenue to Germany's 16 states.
But if a compromise is achieved, that would help open the way for serious debate on government plans to implement a big reform in 1999 of Germany's complex and increasingly inefficient tax system.
Waigel chairs a two-day meeting of his tax reform commission starting on Friday which will examine proposals to cut income tax rates while broadening the revenue base.
He wants a reduction in the top income tax rate to 35 percent from the current 53 percent, while the entry-level rate should fall to around 20 percent from 26 percent now.
The reform would cut the gross tax burden by 80-90 billion marks, to be partly offset by scrapping tax breaks. Taxpayers would end up paying 20-30 billion marks less to the state.

Although Kohl's Free Democrat coalition partners and opposition parties have aired similar tax models, they want the measure to take effect in 1998 -- an election year -- and disagreement is likely on cutting tax breaks.
Most controversial would be eliminating tax breaks on night and weekend work, and making welfare benefits like unemployment pay liable to tax. Both moves are opposed by the SPD.
Companies may also lose chances to avoid taxation by building financial reserves, while investors could face heavier taxation of profits on securities and property dealings.
Waigel's commission is expected to complete its report by December 11.
